explanation: Xoconochco lay hundreds of kilometers from the capital, so goods needed a long journey to get there. That describes a location on the outer edge of the empire, which is what "peripheral" means. "Concealed" and "unobtrusive" suggest being hidden or unnoticed, which has nothing to do with distance from the capital.

The corona brightens before a flare happens, giving an advance warning, so the flare is about to occur, or "impending." "Antecedent" means coming before something, which is the reverse of what's needed, and "innocuous" (harmless) contradicts the description of flares disrupting telecommunications.

Text 1's claim depends on the stone pieces being tools made by humans. Text 2 says it's premature to call them tools, since they may have broken naturally and no other signs of human activity have been found, so Text 2 would say the claim rests on an unsupported assumption. Choice A is wrong because Text 2 doesn't call the claim plausible or discuss a connection between groups.

The underlined line simply notes a wind shaking seed-pods. The speaker then builds on that image, comparing her thoughts to scattered black seeds and describing being "scattered in its whirl," which conveys inner turmoil. Choice A is wrong because the speaker doesn't blame the wind for her feelings; the scene serves as a comparison, not a cause.

The example shows that simple steps like washing footwear can stop invasive organisms from spreading, which means this kind of biodiversity loss can be avoided, or is "preventable." "Concerning" and "common" might be true, but they aren't what the example about simple precautions illustrates.

Text 1 calls the findings "a clear win," showing optimism, while Text 2 welcomes the findings but cautions that effects on food supply must be considered. Choice B is wrong because Text 2 never says 15% is too little; its concern is about food production, not whether the results would be meaningful.

Text 2 agrees the show is outdated but argues it should be kept and points to creative updates such as Hot Chocolate Nutcracker. So the author would answer Text 1's call to stop producing it by suggesting revised versions instead. Choice C overstates Text 2, which never claims most companies could earn more from modernized versions.

The lines describe Aeneas's valor, words, and looks lighting a "secret fire" of love in Dido and being "imprinted in her heart," showing how strongly his story has affected her. The "secret" is her hidden love, not a worry about Aeneas discovering something (D), and nothing suggests she doubts his account (A).

Text 2 warns that animals removing trackers may just be curious about a new object rather than helping. Applied to the magpies, the behavior could be explained without assuming they meant to help. Choice B is wrong because Text 2 says nothing about the birds trying to gain the tracker for themselves.

The text says Cruse managed to disagree with nearly all civil rights thinkers. After the sentence about assimilationists, the underlined sentence shows he also criticized Black nationalists, even though he was one, which explains why he ended up isolated from the whole community. Choice C is wrong because the sentence describes Cruse's own criticism, not a controversy within the nationalist movement.

Text 2 shows the Svalbard bears staying stable despite sea-ice loss by switching to reindeer and eggs, so these researchers would say the extinction prediction ignores the possibility that some populations can adapt. Choice C is wrong because the Svalbard bears have been affected by ice loss; they just adapted to it.

Painters around the world used Velázquez's techniques, so his influence was not limited to Spain, which makes "confined to" the right fit. "Recognized in" doesn't work because "hardly recognized in Spain" would contradict his status as the leading court artist.

The dash explains that a coffee-shop painting of women drinking coffee "may not sound particularly ambitious," so a casual description makes it seem modest, or "unassuming." "Pretentious" means the opposite, suggesting too much ambition.

Text 2 says the countryside, reached through King's Cross, stands for the idealism the novel calls "the infinite." In Text 1, King's Cross suggests Infinity to Margaret and seems a portal to an adventure not measured by ordinary prosperity, so the author would see it as pointing toward the intangible riches of the countryside. Choice A is wrong because Margaret sees King's Cross as a comment against materialism, not a sign of its triumph.

The text says listeners miss Joplin's full creativity by ignoring his less famous works, gives examples, and ends by saying they deserve as much fame as his hits. That is an argument for giving his lesser-known works more attention. Choice A is wrong because ragtime and opera are mentioned only as examples, not compared.
The text names Cardelús as a canopy-soil researcher, explains what canopy soil is and why it matters, and says why she studies it in choibá trees. No disagreement is mentioned, so A and B are wrong.

Latro writes down experiences because he will forget them when he sleeps, so he chooses which ones to keep on record, or "preserve." "Imagine" and "suggest" don't fit, since he is recording real experiences.

The first sentence gives the high opinion the laity and clergy have of Mr. Ely, and the second lists his careful habits, like avoiding arguments and never revealing his own views, which keep that reputation intact. Choice C goes too far: the text never describes a separate private conduct or a reason for hiding a true personality.
Love, April, and the gold hair are "mingled together" like the "blending" of a plant and a perfume, so "mingled" means mixed or combined. None of the other choices matches the image of blending.

The underlined portion lists the challenges the narrator set herself "at night in bed," so it gives examples of what she thinks about at night. Choice C is wrong because these are imagined route puzzles, not directions to a favorite store.

The study challenged the accepted view and found that up to half of hunters were female, so the old view must have been that women's role in hunting was tiny, or "negligible." "Commonplace" would mean the old view agreed with the new finding, so it couldn't have been challenged.

The "but" clause says the artisans don't strictly follow every tradition, which implies that they generally do follow the inherited techniques, so "adhere to" fits. "Experiment with" and "improve on" would not set up the contrast with not observing every tradition.

Each section of the novel is told from a different family member's point of view, so the three perspectives are separate and different, or "distinct." Nothing suggests the perspectives were "required" or "unknown."

Seismic data narrows down the area, and orbital images then pinpoint the crater, so each method supplies what the other lacks; they are "complementary." "Interchangeable" and "redundant" would mean either method could do the job alone, which the text contradicts.

"Generations of mystery and horror writers" is the subject and "have been influenced" is its verb. No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, so the comma, dash, and semicolon in B, C, and D are all wrong.

The words after the blank are a list that names the three periods, and a colon after a complete clause is the standard way to introduce such a list. A and C wrongly treat the list as a complete sentence, and a comma in D doesn't clearly introduce the list.
The verb's subject is "that," which refers to the singular noun "radiation," so it needs the singular verb "occurs." Choices B, C, and D are plural forms and don't agree with "radiation."

Both "The Mission 66 initiative... represented a major investment..." and "it prioritized physical improvements..." are independent clauses, and a semicolon correctly joins them. A comma alone (D) creates a comma splice, while B and A run the clauses together without proper punctuation.

"Entomologist Heather Grab" is the subject of "found," and the title "Entomologist" is essential to the name, so no punctuation belongs between the title and name or between the subject and verb. A, B, and D all add punctuation that wrongly interrupts the sentence.

The opening phrase "Despite being cheap, versatile, and easy to produce" must describe the noun that comes right after it, and that's commercial plastics. Only D places "commercial plastics" there and then uses a colon to introduce the two problems. In A, B, and C, the phrase would describe "there," "two problems," or "two associated problems," none of which is cheap or versatile.

"Where sound is made" is part of a statement describing the mouthpiece, not a direct question, so it keeps normal subject-verb order and ends with a period. Choices A and D add a question mark, and B and D use question word order.

The introductory phrase "After pleading for years... for the passage of key antidiscrimination legislation" describes the people who pleaded, so the activists must come right after the comma. In A, B, and C, the phrase would wrongly describe pressure, a protest, or lawmakers.

The sentence's main verb is "adapted," so the blank must start a phrase describing the scientists: "scientists searching for evidence... adapted the test." Using a finite verb like "searched," "were searching," or "have searched" would leave the sentence with two main verbs and no conjunction joining them.

The text uses present tense ("use an Ease of Living Index") to describe what the tool currently does, so the simple present "measures" fits. The past perfect, conditional, and future perfect forms in B, C, and D don't match that time frame.

There is one phrase, so the singular possessive "phrase's" is correct, and the later pronoun refers back to that single phrase, so it should be "its." A and B use plural or non-possessive forms, and C uses the plural pronoun "their."
The subject is "the country's name," which is singular, so the verb must be the singular "is." The other choices are plural verbs.

The phrase "the cellular organs that generate energy from light" is an interruption that ends with a dash, so it must also begin with a dash. A pair of matching dashes sets it off correctly; a comma or semicolon at the start (B, C) doesn't match the closing dash, and A leaves the opening unmarked.

"Carbon-13 (¹³C)" renames "a rare carbon isotope," so it is an appositive that must be set off with a comma on each side; the comma before it is already in place, so the blank needs a comma after "(¹³C)." B leaves out the closing comma, and A and C wrongly put a comma between "carbon-13" and its abbreviation.

fix.passage: A study led by scientist Rebecca Kirby at the University of Wisconsin–Madison found that black bears that eat human food before hibernation have increased levels of a rare carbon isotope, ______ due to the higher ¹³C levels in corn and cane sugar. Bears with these elevated levels were also found to have much shorter hibernation periods on average.

explanation: The main verb is "assembles," so the words before it must form a modifier set off by commas: "Richard Serra, intending his installations to..., assembles...." A and D add a second main verb, and B puts a comma between the subject "Serra" and the verb "intends."

The sentence states what the researchers investigated, so "how people perceive acts of kindness" is an indirect question that uses statement word order and ends with a period. A and B use question word order, and B and C wrongly end with a question mark.

"The Limón technique... is known for... weight and weightlessness" and "dancers may explore... the moment of mid-air suspension" are both independent clauses, so a semicolon correctly joins them. A runs them together, C is a comma splice, and B creates an ungrammatical clause with "which."

"Among them Nigerian American essayist and novelist Teju Cole..." has no main verb, so it can't stand alone as a sentence. It works as a phrase attached to the main clause with a comma, naming one of the writers. A and C treat the phrase as an independent clause, and B leaves out the needed comma.

The butterfly is flapping its own wings, so the possessive pronoun "its" (no apostrophe) is needed, and "wings" is a plain plural that doesn't own anything. "It's" means "it is," and "wings'" or "wing's" are possessive forms that don't fit here.

The pronoun refers back to "a given industry," which is singular, so "it" with the singular verb "consists" is correct. A and B use plural forms that don't agree with "industry," and "this" in D is unclear and doesn't plainly point to the industry.

The first sentence ends after the parenthetical "(i.e., fungi that live inside a host plant)," and "By researching... she found..." is a new independent clause. A period correctly separates them. A comma (B) creates a comma splice, and C and D run the two independent clauses together.

Buratti was in the middle of studying the data when she "made" the discovery in the past, so the past progressive "was studying" fits. The present, present perfect progressive, and future forms don't match the past-tense "made."

The construction "so bright, so localized, and so dependable that it has become known..." is a single "so...that" structure, so no punctuation should separate "dependable" from "that." A colon, semicolon, or comma would break up that connection.

"Jamaican British artist Willard Wigan is known for his remarkable microsculptures" is a complete sentence, and "Creations so small... Wigan's sculptures are made from tiny natural materials" is another one. A period correctly separates them. B creates a comma splice, while A and D run the two sentences together.

"While one requires oxygen and one does not" is a dependent clause introducing the main clause "aerobic and anaerobic respiration are both forms...," so a comma belongs between them. A period or semicolon (B, D) would leave the dependent clause as a fragment, and A needs a comma to separate the clauses.

"Though" here means "however" and belongs with the first clause: "This has not always been the case, though." The second part, "throughout geologic history, Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places...," is a separate independent clause, so a semicolon must follow "though." A and B create comma splices, and C attaches "though" to the wrong clause.

Rock and rap each have their own chorus-to-verse ratios ("each genre's data"), so this is separate possession, which requires both nouns to be possessive: "rock's and rap's." Choice D shows joint possession, as if the two genres shared one set of ratios, and A and C use plurals instead of possessives.

The opening phrase "Supported by biochemical analyses of over 2,000 skeletons" must describe what comes right after it. Only findings can be supported by analyses, so D is correct. In A, B, and C the phrase would wrongly describe vegetables and grains, the rulers' diets, or the diets' components.

The sentence's main verb is "honors," so the part before it must be a modifier: "Udé, having referred to Nollywood... as '...,' honors its legacy." A and B create a second main verb ("has referred") with nothing joining it to "honors," and C leaves "referred" as a verb that makes the sentence ungrammatical.

The sentence lists three things Belpré did, and because the first item contains commas, the items must be separated by semicolons, matching the semicolon already used before "and put on puppet shows." Only B places a semicolon after the first item, and it keeps "at the time" attached to "an uncommon practice" without extra commas.

"The mechanism by which plants... turn carbon dioxide and water into nutrients" is an appositive that begins with a comma after "Photosynthesis," so it must close with a comma too. A dash in D doesn't match the opening comma, and A and B leave the appositive unclosed.

The phrase "which assume that people are consistently rational decision-makers" ends with a dash before "cannot explain," so it must also begin with a dash after "models." A comma (B) wouldn't match the closing dash, and C and D place the punctuation incorrectly.

The clause "that ___ in parallel arrays" needs a finite verb, and "that" refers to the singular "pattern," so the singular present-tense "results" is correct. "Resulting" and "to result" aren't finite verbs, and "were resulting" is plural.
"Currently" signals the present, so the present-tense "includes" is correct, and it agrees with the singular subject "range." The past, past perfect, and future perfect forms don't match "currently."

Two independent clauses are joined by the conjunction "but," so a comma is needed before it. A creates a comma splice, C runs the clauses together, and B leaves out the comma that should come before "but."

The opening phrase "Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight" describes the people who know this, so "the researchers" must come right after the comma. B makes the researchers' theory the one doing the knowing, and C and D make the moths the knowers.

"Rudolph didn't just walk, she ran—fast" completes one thought, and "During the 1960 Summer Olympics in Rome, she won..." is a new independent clause, so a period is needed after "fast." A, B, and C join the two independent clauses without proper punctuation, creating a run-on or comma splice.

The subject of the verb is "frameworks" (the long phrase in between is just description), which is plural, so it needs the plural verb "underlie." A, B, and D are singular forms that would agree with "person" or "affiliation," not the true subject.

The text describes what happens each night in the present tense ("is bathed," "is"), so the present-tense "illuminates" fits. The future, conditional, and past forms don't match that ongoing present situation.

The subject is "the presence," which is singular; "of many fossilized microbacteria" and the "which" clause just describe it. So the singular verb "reinforces" is correct, while A, C, and D are plural verbs that wrongly agree with "microbacteria."

"Though" here means "however" and finishes the first clause: "Such interpretations are ultimately speculative, though." The next part, "the object's gray coloration may be...," is a separate independent clause, so a semicolon must follow "though." A and D create comma splices, and C wrongly attaches "though" to the second clause.

The opening phrase "Based on events that occurred when Rabinal was a city-state" must describe what immediately follows it. The thing based on events is the drama, so "Rabinal Achí" must come right after the comma, as in A. B, C, and D place a military leader or "there" in that spot, which wrongly makes the person "based on events."

The subject is the gerund phrase "Amplifying the voices and experiences of Black soldiers," which counts as one singular activity, so it takes the singular verb "was." The past tense also matches the Civil War setting. A, B, and C are plural forms that wrongly agree with "soldiers."
The events took place in 1903, and the text uses past tense ("guided," "upheld"), so the simple past "vowed" is correct. The present and future forms don't fit this past narrative.

The sentence needs a main verb for the subject "embryos," and the present-tense plural "enter" fits the general fact being described. "To enter," "having entered," and "entering" aren't main verbs, so they would leave the sentence incomplete.

The subject "Some historians" needs a main verb, and "claim" provides one in the present tense. "Claiming," "having claimed," and "to claim" can't serve as main verbs, so they would leave the sentence a fragment.

"Which" refers to "the Nerf football," a single item that still exists, so it takes the singular present verb "is" and the singular noun "version." A and C use the plural "were," and B and C use the plural "versions."

"That" in the opening phrase stands for an HHI score ("that of a highly concentrated market"), so the comparison must be with another HHI score: "the HHI score of a less concentrated market." A and D compare a score with a market, and C compares it with a clause, which are illogical comparisons.
The clause needs a main verb for the subject "yellow," and the present-tense "is" fits the present-day description of modern color theory. "Having been," "to be," and "being" can't act as main verbs.

"By the end of the 1990s" marks a point in the past before which the doubling was complete, so the past perfect "had doubled" is correct. The present perfect, present, and future forms don't fit a completed past action.

"Chemistry professor" works as a title right before the name, so no comma belongs between "professor" and "Yugang Sun." The full subject is "chemistry professor Yugang Sun and his colleagues," so no comma should come before "and" either. B, C, and D add commas that break up the subject.

The text describes a general process in the present tense ("travel," "are diverted"), so the present-tense "reach" fits after "until." "Will reach" and "had reached" shift tense, and "are reaching" doesn't fit a single moment of hitting the energy level.

The blank is paired with "pack" in the present tense ("the Sherpas pack up... and ___ ready") to describe what the team habitually does, so the present-tense "get" is needed. The past forms in B, C, and D break the parallel with "pack."

The writings belong to one author, Paine, so the singular possessive "author's" is needed, and "writings" is a simple plural with no apostrophe. A lacks the apostrophe, C makes "writing's" possessive, and D uses a plural possessive for a single author.
The subject "the vest frottoir" is singular, and the text describes it in the present tense, so "is" is correct. A, C, and D are plural verb forms.

"By 2023" refers to a point in the past by which her rise to fame was complete, so the past perfect "had become" fits. "Will become" and "will have become" refer to the future, and "becomes" is present tense.
